title: Pelvic organ prolapse
intro: Pelvic organ prolapse happens when the bladder, womb or bowel bulge down into the vagina because the supporting muscles and tissues have weakened. It is common, especially after childbirth and menopause. Many women have only mild symptoms, and treatment ranges from exercises and pessaries to surgery.

sections.heading: Causes and risk factors
paragraphs: Vaginal childbirth, especially with large babies or assisted delivery, is the main risk factor. Others include ageing and menopause, being overweight, chronic cough, long-standing constipation with straining, heavy lifting and family history. Prolapse may affect the front wall (bladder), the back wall (bowel), or the womb itself.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Women often feel heaviness or dragging in the pelvis, a bulge at or beyond the vaginal opening, difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel, urine leakage, recurrent urinary infections or discomfort during sex. Symptoms are often worse at the end of the day or after standing and ease when lying down.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: A doctor examines the pelvis while you are lying and sometimes while you strain or stand, to grade the prolapse. Tests of bladder function or imaging are only needed in selected cases. Not all prolapse needs treatment; the aim is to relieve bothersome symptoms.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Pelvic floor muscle training, lifestyle measures such as weight loss and treating constipation, and a vaginal pessary are first-line options. Vaginal oestrogen helps after menopause. Surgery is considered when symptoms are bothersome and other approaches fail or are not wanted. Operations repair the weakened walls, lift the womb or remove it, or close the vagina in older women who no longer want intercourse. Mesh is used less often because of complications.
Surgery carries risks such as infection, bladder or bowel injury and recurrence, and some women need a repeat operation.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Pelvic floor exercises during and after pregnancy, avoiding constipation and straining, stopping smoking, treating chronic cough and keeping a healthy weight help lower the risk or slow progression.

examples.title: Preparing for a visit
examples.text: Imagine you feel a bulge when you stand for a long time. You could note when symptoms occur, how they affect work and intimacy, and which treatments you would consider before your appointment.

examples.title: Comparing options
examples.text: Suppose your gynaecologist offers a pessary or surgery. You might ask about success rates, risks and recovery for each, and whether you can start with the less invasive option.
